the Middle East has also contributed. Global
observed oil inventories were drawn down at an
average rate of about 2.4 million barrels a day
(mb/d) from March to September, helping to
buffer a persistent production deficit (figure 1.B). Global oil consumption has nonetheless proved
responsive to higher prices, declining by 5 mb/d
(y/y) in 2026Q2 and 3.7 mb/d in Q3.

The Middle East conflict has dealt a historic shock to energy supplies, but several other shocks are also hitting
commodity markets. Hostilities between Russia and Ukraine are impeding Black Sea grain and oilseed
shipments and constraining Russia’s output of oil products, notably diesel. A very strong El Niño threatens the
production of agricultural commodities. In addition, supply constraints amid demand from renewables- and
technology-linked investment have propelled base metals prices higher. Overall, commodity prices are projected
to increase by 23 percent in 2026, to their second-highest level since 2013, led by a 32 percent jump in energy
prices. As global oil production drops more than 5 percent in 2026, Brent oil prices are forecast to remain
elevated in the near term, averaging $91 per barrel for the year.

The state of commodity markets
The outlook for commodity markets has become
increasingly complex amid potentially reinforcing
shocks related to multiple conflict fronts and an
unusually powerful El Niño. Crude oil exports
from the Gulf region have recently been close to
preconflict volumes, aided by pipeline flows and
workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers beyond
the Strait of Hormuz. Nonetheless, flows of
refined oil products from the region have
remained depressed amid damage to refineries, at
less than half of preconflict levels in September. Meanwhile attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West
Pipeline and threats to shipping in the Red Sea
highlight the potential vulnerability of alternative
export routes for crude oil that helped to attenuate
disruptions this year.

Several
producers outside the Gulf have ramped up
output, collectively adding nearly 2.2 mb/d, on
average, since the conflict began, while trading
patterns have adjusted to connect importers
usually dependent on the Gulf with alternative
suppliers. In 2026Q2, during the deepest supply
shortfalls in the Middle East, shifts in oil trade in
the United States and China illustrated these
trends. U.S. exports of crude oil and oil products
increased by about 1.7 mb/d relative to February,
enabled by inventory releases and a pickup in
production, while China’s imports declined by
more than 5 mb/d as refinery runs fell and oil
stocks were drawn (figure 1.C). The global oil
production surplus last year, which exceeded 2
mb/d in 2025Q4, also reduced the extent of the
adjustments to global demand (figure 1.D).

Oil prices would be higher still if oil demand
were not set to fall 2.5 percent this year, the third-largest drop behind the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and
the oil crisis in 1980. Food commodity prices are on track to climb by 10 percent in 2026, well above the April
forecast. Metal and minerals prices are projected to reach an all-time high. In 2027, commodity prices are
forecast to decline by 7 percent, with Brent prices receding to $79 per barrel and slight reductions in other
energy and metal prices, but a further 7 percent rise in food prices. Even so, 2027 price projections have mostly
been revised up since April, by 14 percent for energy.

The forecast hinges on a confluence of moderating factors:
no major escalation of the Middle East conflict, a recovery in Russia’s oil output, easing constraints on Black Sea
food shipments, and manageable crop losses from El Niño. Setbacks on these fronts could mean persistently high
energy prices and stress in food markets. In an adverse scenario, oil prices would average $105 per barrel in
2027, and food prices would exceed their 2022 level. Such developments would drive global inflation higher
and worsen food insecurity.

As the Middle East conflict has extended, and with
the Northern Hemisphere winter coming into
view, upward pressure has mounted on natural gas
prices in economies dependent on liquefied
natural gas (LNG) imports. By mid-October,
European natural gas prices, which are largely
determined by spot LNG prices, had nearly tripled
from preconflict levels. Although LNG transits
through the Strait of Hormuz have recently started
to increase, far fewer LNG vessels than crude
tankers have transited since the June
memorandum of understanding between the
Islamic Republic of Iran and the United States did
not produce a follow-on agreement. Even with
improved flows in September, LNG shipments
were estimated at only about one quarter of
pre-conflict cargoes.

Variation in
connectedness can reflect global shocks that trigger
common commodity price reactions, or
idiosyncratic shocks that induce changes via
substitution or complementarity relationships, or
supply chain connections. Linkages that transmit
price volatility from one commodity to others
(transmitted connectedness) tend to become more
pronounced when economic or commodity
market stress episodes arise, including following
the start of the current Middle East conflict (figure
3.B). On average, industrial metals transmit the
most volatility to other commodity groups, likely
because they are a bellwether for broader economic
cycles (figure 3.C).

At the onset of the Middle East
conflict the primary transmitters of price volatility
were oil and aluminum, both subject to direct
supply disruptions, while precious metals also
played a prominent role amid geopolitical strains
(figure 3.D). FIGURE 2 Recent price pressures and volatility in

More
broadly, structural conditions for a sustained spell
of elevated base metal prices appear to be in place
as global investment transitions toward more
base-metal-intensive sectors and supply growth
remains relatively limited. For precious metals,
pronounced geopolitical and policy uncertainty
continues to sustain high prices, amid marked
volatility (figure 2.D). Gold, silver, and platinum
prices regained upward momentum starting in
July, lifting average January to September prices
for 2026 by 42, 71, and 110 percent, respectively. Beyond the drivers of individual commodity
prices, commodity market connectedness—
defined as the extent to which the volatility of one
commodity price can be explained by shocks to
other commodity prices—has shifted over time
(special focus; figure 3.A).

Global
economic growth is assumed to remain moderate,
in line with the recent consensus among private
sector forecasters, while investment in sectors like
data centers and renewables—important drivers of
metal demand—is expected to remain robust. On
this basis, the World Bank Group’s commodity
price index is forecast to increase by 23 percent in
2026 (y/y), reaching its second-highest level since
2013, before prices retreat by 7 percent in 2027
(figure 4.A; table 1).1

In the baseline, energy prices are set to increase by
32 percent (y/y) this year, then retreat by 12

projected energy prices have been revised higher
by 7 percent for 2026 and 14 percent for 2027,
reflecting longer but less intense Middle East
supply disruptions.

crude shipments from the Gulf is assumed to

crude supplies are expected to ease market

projected 58 percent (y/y) this year to $19 per

in 2026 before retreating by 7 percent in 2027 . The recovery of global
oil consumption in 2027 is projected to be tepid, partly because an
accelerated shift to electric vehicles is likely to have a lasting effect. Oil
demand is therefore expected to substantially lag its 2010–19 trend in the

than four decades outside the 2020 global
recession. Modest increases in oil output in
advanced economies, such as Canada and the
United States, as well as in Latin America and the
Caribbean, are on track to offset only a small share
of very large production losses in the Middle East
(figure 4.C). Next year, operational adaptations
that have facilitated increased crude oil exports
from the Gulf region in recent months are
assumed to remain effective, allowing shipments to
continue gradually building. A recovery in the
global production of refined products is likely to

Adverse weather
conditions related to El Niño have also disrupted
the planting and harvesting of rice and sugar, for
which 2027 price forecasts have been revised up by
21 percent and 12 percent, respectively. Next year’s
projected average cocoa price, while still well
below the 2025 level, has also been raised by
nearly 30 percent since April. Despite substantial challenges for a subset of
commodities, the overall impact of El Niño on
food commodity prices is expected to be
manageable, consistent with historical experience
(figure 4.D). At the global level, price pressures are
likely to be mitigated by the varied nature of the
related weather effects, which can lift production
in some locations while hindering it in others. Solid harvests in aggregate for key crops are also
likely to help contain price increases.

In
2027, food commodity prices are forecast to climb
by another 7 percent, led by a 9 percent rise in
grain prices. This mainly reflects headwinds to rice
production in Asia and wheat production globally,
generally related to deteriorating growing
conditions, in some cases because of El Niño. Oils
and meals prices are projected to increase by 8
percent, driven by soybean-derived products
because of robust demand for animal feed and
biofuels, as well as El Niño-related curbs on palm
oil production.

Beverage prices are expected to retreat by 24
percent (y/y) in 2026, as both cocoa and coffee
production recover from past disease- and
weather-related declines. Average beverage prices
are forecast to broadly stabilize thereafter, as
declining coffee prices partly offset a pickup in
cocoa prices. In all, the World Bank Group’s
agricultural commodity price index—a composite
measure for food, beverages, and raw materials—is
forecast to inch up this year, then gain 5 percent in
2027. The effects of El Niño are evident in several price
forecast revisions relative to April 2026. The palm
oil price forecast, for instance, has been revised
higher by 15 percent in 2027 amid unusually dry
conditions in Indonesia.

LNG production is more
concentrated in economies heavily affected by the
conflict than oil production, and natural gas
output in the Middle East is expected to remain
below its 2025 level in 2027, in large part because
of damage to LNG trains in Qatar. Although
natural gas production is projected to expand
elsewhere next year, global demand is also
anticipated to recover, such that Asian and
European markets remain notably tight. Meanwhile, U.S. natural gas prices are forecast to
increase by 6 percent in 2027 from much lower
levels, partly owing to increasing LNG export
demand. Coal prices are on course to climb by 25 percent
(y/y) in 2026 on stronger demand and supply
constraints.

although global grain output is anticipated to drop

14 percent (y/y) in 2026, mainly reflecting a surge

among other factors (figure 4.E). Some other

The metals and minerals index is projected
to edge 3 percent (y/y) lower in 2027 as supply
conditions improve somewhat for several base
metals owing to fading production or export
disruptions and new capacity coming on stream. For copper, however, mined supply growth
is anticipated to remain subdued, reflecting
factors such as declining ore grades in Chile,
the world’s largest producer. Assuming global
economic growth holds up, buoyant base metal
demand driven by, for example, the expansion of
renewable energy infrastructure, electric vehicles,
and data centers is likely to keep medium-term
prices elevated (figure 4.F). Precious metal prices are also expected to register a
steep average increase of 40 percent in 2026, amid
strong demand for diversifying financial assets
against a strained geopolitical backdrop.

infrastructure or more strikes on ships in the Red

to the Middle East. Although Russia’s exports are
assumed to be unconstrained next year in the
baseline, damage to its infrastructure meaningfully
reduced oil product exports in 2026Q3 (figure
5.A). If outages at oil facilities in Russia continue
at their recent frequency, global oil production
could further undershoot projected consumption,
with diesel shortages a particular concern. Any
worsening of oil export prospects in the Middle

El Niño affects agricultural commodity markets
predominantly by changing temperature and precipitation in major producing regions. Drought or excess
rainfall reduces crop output, while flooding disrupts
harvesting, storage, and transport.

El Niño also affects
non-agricultural commodity markets. Drought reduces
hydropower generation, constrains mining operations,
and disrupts shipping corridors such as the Panama
Canal. Heavy rainfall disrupts open-pit mining, road
transport, and logistics, while warmer conditions raise
electricity demand for cooling. These effects raise
production and transport costs and propagate through
supply chains. While El Niño’s reach is global, its effects can be highly
localized. About two-thirds of countries in Sub-Saharan
Africa (SSA) and Latin America and the Caribbean
(LAC), and half of those in East Asia and Pacific
(EAP), are highly exposed to El Niño.

Episodes of El Niño vary considerably in intensity
(figure B1.2.A).a Since 1950, there have been 27 El
Niño episodes, four of which were very strong (in
1982–83, 1991–92, 1997–98, and 2015–16), with the
current episode expected to become the fifth. Over the
same period, there were 3 strong, 9 moderate, and 11
weak episodes. El Niño episodes typically emerge
around May or June, strengthen through the third
quarter of the year, peak near year-end, and dissipate
during the first half of the following year. As a result,
much of the associated rainfall anomaly occurs during
the second half of the year, overlapping with the
growing season for several major internationally traded
commodities.

BOX 1 The 2026-27 El Niño: Implications for commodity markets
El Niño, a major recurring source of global weather variability, alters rainfall and temperature patterns over a large
geographical area, with consequences for commodity markets. The current episode, expected to reach very strong intensity
and persist into early 2027, is likely to have a moderate effect on aggregate global food commodity price indexes, but could
substantially affect individual commodities. The largest effects are likely for commodities whose exports are concentrated in
highly exposed countries, such as rice, soybeans, palm oil, coffee, and cocoa, which have historically experienced some of the
largest price increases following El Niño conditions.

Remote links between ENSO and distant weather patterns,
known as teleconnections, are typically measured by correlations
between an ENSO index and local temperature and precipitation, and
are generally strongest in the tropics. This box uses the country-level
teleconnection metric of Callahan and Mankin (2023), based on correlations between eastern Pacific ENSO variability (also known as the
E-index) and monthly temperature and precipitation over 1960–2019,

Potential implications of the current El Niño

The World Bank Group’s food commodity price index
is forecast to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and a further 7
percent in 2027, representing upward revisions of 8
and 14 percent, respectively, from the April 2026
Commodity Markets Outlook. These revisions reflect
tighter market conditions and the materialization of
several downside supply risks, including the prolonged
conflict in the Middle East and disruptions to Black
Sea grain shipments. El Niño conditions have also
prompted substantial upward revisions to forecasts for
several commodities.

El Niño is estimated to raise global nonenergy commodity prices by about 5 percent over 6–16 months (Cashin,
Mohaddes, and Raissi 2017). The strongest evidence of price effects is for
tropical agricultural products, including vegetable oils, oilseeds, coffee,
and cocoa, with weaker effects for grains and metals (Ubilava 2018).

Relatively favorable supply
conditions, on the other hand, are helping to contain
price increases for some grains, as global grain markets
entered the current El Niño episode with more
adequate supplies than during previous price spikes,
such as in 2007-08. The aggregate stocks-to-use ratio (a
rough measure of supply relative to demand) for grains
is expected to be nearly 28 percent in 2026-27, similar
to the 30-year average of 27.7 percent and well above
the 18.1 percent recorded in 2007-08. Excluding
China, the ratio is expected to reach 17.2 percent in
2026-27, still above the 15 percent recorded in
2007-08 (figure B1.3.E). Global food markets could
tighten if El Niño coincided with further trade disruptions, including additional restrictions on Black Sea
grain exports and renewed export controls by major
exporters.

Recent developments
Nitrogen (urea) prices averaged $399/mt in
2026Q3, down 42 percent (q/q) and 18 percent
(y/y), after peaking at $857/mt in April (figure

October. The initial retreat during 2026Q2
reflected China’s easing of export restrictions in
May, the temporary reduction in hostilities

China and other major suppliers, including Egypt,
Nigeria, and Oman, helped sustain a return to
more normal price levels.

DAP (diammonium phosphate) prices rose by 4
percent in 2026Q3 (q/q), extending the 20
percent increase in 2026Q2 to narrowly exceed
their year-earlier level. Conflict-related shortages
of sulfur, a key input in the production of DAP ,
due to disruptions in the Middle East continued
to constrain supply, although shortages began to
ease in October as sulfur shipments reportedly
crossed the Strait of Hormuz. Prices of ammonia,
another key input of DAP , remained 8 percent
higher in September than a year earlier, with 15
percent of global ammonia trade also disrupted by
developments in the Strait (figure 18.C). European
natural gas prices, at 91 percent higher than a year
earlier in 2026Q3, have raised ammonia
production costs for suppliers in Europe.

China’s urea exports are expected to reach 7.0
million metric tons (mmt) in 2026, up from 4.9
mmt in 2025. Although an export ban imposed
after the start of the Middle East conflict cut
exports to near zero between March and June,
China’s urea exports in the first eight months of
2026 matched the level of a year earlier, at about
1.4 mmt, with two-thirds shipped in July and
August (figure 18.B). This ramp-up of exports
helped replace a sizable portion of supplies
blocked by the initial near closure of the Strait of
Hormuz. It also highlights China’s potential role as
a swing supplier, given its large coal-based urea
industry, accumulated inventories previously
under export restrictions, and capacity additions in
2026.

negligible, and as potash is mined rather than

supported by the easing of U.S. sanctions on
Belarus, the third-largest producer after Canada
and Russia. As a result, MOP remains the most

text:
Using a measure of price
volatility connectedness across 15 internationally traded commodities over 2006–26, commodity-specific factors
are found to dominate price volatility: roughly two-thirds is commodity-specific, while about one-third is
associated with shocks in other commodity markets. About half of measured connectedness reflects links within
broad commodity groups. Industrial metals and food are the principal net-transmitting groups, while livestock
and soft commodities are the main net receivers. At the individual commodity level, copper, maize, oil, and
silver stand out as important bridges across groups.

text:
Price
volatility connectedness measures how much of
the variance in a commodity’s price volatility can
be explained by shocks affecting prices in other
commodity markets. The methodology applies the
Diebold-Yilmaz connectedness framework to
estimate how much volatility is transmitted across
commodities and how these relationships evolve
over time (Diebold and Yilmaz 2009, 2012, 2014;
Demirer et al. 2018). The analysis addresses the
following questions:
• How extensive is commodity price
connectedness within and across commodity
groups? • Which individual commodities play
particularly important roles in linking
otherwise distinct commodity groups? • How does commodity price connectedness
change during episodes of global stress?

Introduction
Commodity prices often move in tandem because
many markets are exposed to common shifts in
global activity, input costs, trade, and financial
conditions. For instance, a slowdown in industrial
activity can weaken demand for energy and
industrial metals at the same time, while
disruptions to energy supply can raise transport
and fertilizer costs and spill into agricultural
markets. Periods of financial or geopolitical stress
can broaden these movements across otherwise
distinct commodity groups (World Bank 2024).

metadata.section: Special Focus Commodity Price Connections: How Does Volatility Spread?

text:
Understanding these linkages is key because
commodity price shocks affect inflation, fiscal
revenues, trade balances, and food and energy
security, particularly in emerging market and
developing economies (EMDEs) with large
commodity exposures (Balcilar, Usman and Agan
2024; World Bank 2026a). Most commodity
analysis appropriately focuses on the supply and
demand fundamentals of individual markets. While that approach remains important, it
provides only a partial view when volatility
associated with one commodity is linked to
developments in other commodity markets. This Special Focus examines price volatility
connectedness across 15 internationally traded
commodities in six groups—energy, food,
industrial metals, livestock, precious metals, and
soft commodities (such as coffee and cotton)—
using daily data from 2006 to 2026.

permanent transmission hub. Taken together, these findings suggest that analysis
of individual commodity-market fundamentals

Crops compete
for the same land, water, fertilizer, and transport
capacity and are linked to one another through
feed demand and biofuel margins. A disturbance
to one crop can consequently propagate to the
others through the reallocation of acreage and
inputs, and beyond agriculture through fuel and
feed markets. T ransmission in this case may
operate closer to a resource-constraint channel,
which helps explain why two groups with little in
common in terms of fundamentals both register as
principal net transmitters (Karkowska and Urjasz
2024). Livestock and soft commodities are at the other
end of the spectrum, with more of their volatility
associated with shocks arriving from elsewhere
than with volatility transmitted outward.

Industrial
metals and food have net connectedness indexes of
about 11 and 7, respectively, and their transmitted

soft commodities have net indexes of
approximately −4 and −8 and transmit only about
half as much volatility as they receive. Industrial metals and food occupy the same end of
the ranking for different reasons, and the
distinction matters for how their roles should be
interpreted. Industrial metals’ transmitting role
may partly reflect the structure of their markets. Deep, globally integrated trading facilitates rapid
price adjustment, potentially supporting
transmission across commodity markets beyond
direct production-chain linkages (Tiwari et al. 2022). Food commodities transmit volatility
through a different mechanism.

transmission is broadly shared among constituent

Connectedness during episodes
of global stress
Connectedness varies over time, rising during
major global stress episodes and receding as
pressures ease and commodity-specific
fundamentals regain importance. The total
connectedness index averages about 43 during the
global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic,
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the recent
Middle East conflict, compared with 32 outside of
these events.5 During global stress episodes,
common shocks—including those related to global
activity, financial conditions, risk appetite, and
transport costs—account for more commodity
price volatility. As pressures ease, inventories,
harvests, local supply conditions, and other
commodity-specific fundamentals reassert
themselves and connectedness recedes.

Industrial metals record the largest increase in
received connectedness during COVID-19 and
the Middle East conflict, while food’s exposure
rises most sharply during COVID-19. Even
relatively self-contained groups, such as livestock
and soft commodities, become more integrated
during periods of global stress. Net connectedness reveals persistent roles but also
shifts between transmission and absorption
(figures SF .3.E and SF .3.F). Industrial metals
remain net transmitters in every stress episode,
while food became a net receiver during
COVID-19, illustrating how an increase in
outward transmission can coexist with a net
receiving position. Energy and precious metals are
net transmitters during COVID-19 but net
receivers in the other episodes.

metadata.section: Special Focus Commodity Price Connections: How Does Volatility Spread?

text:
Greater connectedness during global stress reflects
both stronger commodity-market linkages and
shifts among transmitting and receiving groups. T ransmission rises across groups, led by industrial
metals, especially during COVID-19 and the
Middle East conflict (figures SF .3.A and SF .3.B). Food transmission remains consistently high but
shows fewer stress-related spikes, while
transmission from energy and precious metals rose
particularly sharply during COVID-19. Livestock
and soft commodities remain marginal despite
higher transmission during stress. Global stress also broadens exposure to external
volatility, with received connectedness above
non-stress levels for every group (figures SF .3.C
and SF .3.D). Energy and precious metals absorb
substantial amounts of volatility across all four
episodes while also transmitting volatility.

metadata.section: Special Focus Commodity Price Connections: How Does Volatility Spread?

text:
Metal consumption responds
strongly to industrial production, as demand
shocks tend to be more important drivers of metal
prices than supply shocks (Stuermer 2018; World
Bank 2021). For this reason, major movements in
metal prices can provide insights about the state of
the global economy, especially during periods of
heightened economic volatility (Matsumoto,
Pescatori and Wang 2023). As metal markets
reflect changes in demand extending beyond the
consumption of metals, their prices can provide
information about the broader economy and
stress. Pivotality in the commodity system is
therefore not a single attribute: it reflects either a
standing position between two groups or an
episodic increase in the importance of channels
that are otherwise latent.

during COVID-19 occurred as transport demand
collapsed and global portfolios rebalanced. Livestock and soft commodities remain net

net absorption increasing particularly sharply
during COVID-19. Differences in the economic setting may help
explain how connectedness varies across periods of
global stress. Global demand disturbances tend to

conditions. Supply disruptions and geopolitical
shocks can strengthen connectedness in markets
most directly exposed to these shocks, while
portfolio reallocation can increase the prominence

Niño on wheat prices (box 1). Physical links provide plausible explanations for
the larger increases in maize and soybean
transmission. Maize supplies livestock feed and
ethanol, while soybean crushing produces soymeal
for feed and soyoil for food and biofuels. Uncertainty about either crop’s availability can
alter feed costs, substitution between ingredients,
and biofuel feedstock costs. Competition for land
provides another connection: farmers can
reallocate acreage as relative profitability changes,

text:
The results indicate that the strong phase of the
2015-16 El Niño was associated with much larger
increases in transmitted connectedness than the
weak phase (figure SF .4.B). Soybeans recorded the
largest increase in connectedness during the strong
phase, followed by maize. During the weak phase,
maize transmission was broadly unchanged, while
the increase for soybeans was similar to that for
non-food commodities. Wheat transmission
declined in both phases, but more sharply during
the weak phase. Because connectedness is
measured in relative terms, this decline indicates
that wheat price volatility had less influence on
other markets than did maize and soybean price
volatility, or that market-specific shocks became
more important (Diebold and Yilmaz 2012).

metadata.section: Special Focus Commodity Price Connections: How Does Volatility Spread?

text:
This is
consistent with the broader finding that precious
metals can act as conduits within the commodity
system: they respond to global risk conditions as
well as commodity-specific fundamentals, and, in
doing so, transmit those conditions onward. The 2015-16 El Niño episode
El Niño, the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern
Oscillation (ENSO), is a major source of weather
variability affecting food and other commodity
markets. Episodes vary widely in intensity, and
only a minority—eight out of 26 episodes since
1950—have been classified as strong or very
strong.6 Commodity prices are higher during
ENSO episodes than during neutral periods (box
1). However, price sensitivity differs from volatility
transmission: a large movement in a commodity’s
own price does not necessarily make it a stronger
source of volatility for other markets.

energy inputs and is visible in oil and aluminum,
whose trade and production are exposed to
shipping disruptions through the Straif of Hormuz

of precious metals is consistent with a financial
channel operating alongside physical supply
disruptions, as geopolitical stress can prompt
portfolio reallocation toward assets perceived as
safe havens (Baur and Smales 2020). This channel
is visible in gold and silver, whose transmitted
connectedness rose considerably despite no direct
physical exposure to the disruption.

Broad shocks raise cross-market transmission
during periods of stress, but the groups and
commodities that become most important vary
with the nature of the episode. The commodity
system therefore has a recognizable underlying
structure without a single permanent hub. The
structure of that system is best understood in
terms of how shocks travel rather than where they
originate. Some markets appear to transmit
because they price global conditions early and are
read as signals; others because they share physical
inputs and constraints with neighboring markets;
and a small number bridge otherwise distinct
groups either continuously, by virtue of serving
two sets of end-users, or episodically, when latent
channels become binding.

Industrial metals and food are the principal
net-transmitting groups, whereas livestock and soft
commodities are predominantly net receivers. Energy and precious metals are more balanced
conduits. At the individual-market level, copper,
maize, oil, and silver stand out as important
bridges across commodity groups, although the
persistence and timing of their roles differ. Connectedness also intensifies and reconfigures
during episodes of global stress. The recent Middle
East conflict illustrates this: disruptions to
shipping through the Strait of Hormuz raised
transmitted connectedness most for aluminum,
oil, gold, silver, and wheat, reflecting both a
physical channel operating through energy and
fertilizer costs and a financial channel operating
through portfolio shifts toward safe-haven assets.

Distinguishing among
these mechanisms can help in assessing which
disturbances are likely to remain contained and
which are likely to be associated with broader
cross-market adjustment. These findings suggest that policymakers in
EMDEs should continue to undertake detailed
analysis of supply, demand, inventories, trade,
logistics, and policy conditions in individual
markets, but this analysis can be complemented by
close monitoring of cross-market transmission,
particularly during episodes of stress. This
perspective may be especially relevant for EMDEs
that are highly exposed to commodity prices
through inflation, fiscal revenues, external
balances, or food and energy security.

Commodity prices are connected but far from
fully integrated. Over the past two decades, about
one-third of price volatility has been associated

roughly two-thirds remained commodity specific. Moreover, about half of measured connectedness

APPENDIX SF.1 Methodological
approach
Underlying VAR model and variance
decomposition
The assessment of connectedness between
commodity markets is based on the framework
developed by Diebold and Yilmaz (2012, 2014),
which quantifies the extent to which shocks in one
market or commodity influence others within a
multivariate system. The Diebold and Yilmaz
connectedness metrics are derived from the
forecast error variance decomposition of an elastic
net VAR model of the range-based realized
volatility of the prices for 15 components of the
Bloomberg Commodity Index over the period
ranging from May 5, 2006, to June 26, 2026.

Variance decomposition
The decomposition of the forecast-error variance
of the VAR model was used to quantify the
contribution of shocks in one commodity to the
forecast-error variance of other commodities. The
generalized forecast error variance decomposition
(GFEVD) approach of Pesaran and Shin (1998)
and Koop et al. (1996) is used in this study. The
GFEVD, which relies on a largely data-based
identification scheme, is invariant to variable
ordering. It allows for correlated shocks while
accounting for the historical correlation observed
among them. The entry on the ith row and jth
column of the H-step generalized variance
decomposition matrix D gH denotes the fraction of
the H-step-ahead forecast error variance of variable
i attributable to shocks in variable j.
